messages.subject: Usermodel versus commonfactorGWAS model
parts:

I ran a user model constraining variance of Factor 1 (this is a 3 trait, 1 common factor model, with SNPs) because with the CommonFactorGWAS there were more than a small subset of SNPS with Lavaan warnings:

The output for same snps with unconstrained CommonfactorGWAS model:

2 rs3131972   1 752721 0.161034  A  G 2  F1  ~ SNP  0.0020014544 0.004403527  0.4545117     0.6494606 2.402381    2 0.3008358    0       0

So the Z and Pval estimates are very similar.  

Why are the Est and SE values different - actually all close to a factor of 3.9 (but not all the same).  Is there some standardization process that I am missing?  

I would appreciate any help you can give me.

Best,
Dan

parts:
Regarding the same, I am a little confused.  

I ran the Usermodel version with the model as follows specifed:
model <-'F1 =~ NA*CADR + STROKE + MDD 
F1~~1*F1
F1 ~ SNP'
cf_1test<-userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = p_sumstats_1test, model = model, sub="F1~SNP")

I looked for the SNPS that came up with the Lavaan warning in the unconstrained model (commonfactorGWAS).  In the Usermodel (with constraints) all the same snps came up with this warning (and NAs for est, se, etc):

This particular run produced negative (residual) variances for either your latent or observed variables. You may discard the run for this SNP, re-run the model with constraints to keep variances above 0, or specify an alternative model.

Not sure what I am doing wrong here except that the model didn't work, or I need an alternative model to avoid the Lavaan warnings.

Thanks,
Dan

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: Usermodel versus commonfactorGWAS model
parts:
Hi Dan, 

I'll say two things that might help clear things up:
1. I think the warning you are getting has to do with negative residual variances of one of your observed variables, so you are troubleshooting by putting a constraint on the factor variance, but it seems unlikely that would be issue. 

2. The behavior you are observing in your first message is what I would expect based on the changes you are making. More specifically, we would expect the ratio of estimate/SE to be the same irrespective of how things are scaled, which is why you get equivalent p-values. However, the scale of the betas is going to change in concordance with how you change other parts of the model. So if you fix a factor variance at 2 instead of 1 then you would expect that the betas would increase proportionately. Since we care about p-values in GWAS, and that is consistent, it's typically not a cause for concern how the betas are scaled as long as the ratio of beta/SE is consistent as you are observing. 

Best, 
  Andrew
